name: Photo Response Non-Uniformity
description: Analyzes PRNU-based sensor fingerprint using photo response non-uniformity for camera source identification (Lukáš et al., 2006).
mechanism:
This method leverages Photo Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) — the unique pixel-level sensitivity variation of each camera sensor — as a device fingerprint for source identification and forgery detection:

1. **PRNU Fingerprint Estimation**: The sensor's PRNU fingerprint K is estimated from N reference images {I₁, ..., I_N} captured by the same camera. For each image, a noise residual Wᵢ = Iᵢ − F(Iᵢ) is extracted using a denoising filter F (BM3D). The PRNU is estimated via maximum-likelihood: K̂ = (Σᵢ Wᵢ·Iᵢ) / (Σᵢ Iᵢ²). This multiplicative model accounts for the fact that PRNU scales with signal intensity. A minimum of N = 50 reference images is recommended for reliable estimation, with convergence improving with image diversity.

2. **Camera Source Identification**: For a test image I_test, the noise residual W_test is extracted and correlated with the camera fingerprint K̂. The detection statistic is the Peak-to-Correlation Energy (PCE): PCE = ρ²_peak / ((1/|Ω|) Σ_{(s,t)∈Ω} ρ²(s,t)), where ρ_peak is the maximum normalized cross-correlation and Ω excludes a small neighborhood around the peak. Under H₀ (image not from this camera), PCE follows approximately a central chi-squared distribution. A PCE > 60 indicates the image was captured by the reference camera with false positive probability < 10⁻⁵.

3. **Tampering Localization**: The image is divided into blocks of size B×B (typically 128×128 or 64×64). For each block, the local correlation between W_test and K̂·I_test is computed. Authentic blocks produce high correlation values, while tampered blocks (spliced, inpainted, or AI-generated) show near-zero or negative correlation. A binary tampering map is generated by thresholding the block-level correlation using a Neyman-Pearson criterion at a specified false alarm rate.

4. **AI-Generated Image Detection**: AI-generated images (from GANs, diffusion models, etc.) categorically lack PRNU patterns because they are synthesized computationally rather than captured by a physical sensor. The method tests the global PRNU correlation: authentic photographs produce PCE >> 60, while AI-generated images consistently produce PCE < 10. This provides a highly reliable, physics-based distinction between photographed and synthesized content.
parameters:
Denoising filter: BM3D
Reference images for estimation: ≥ 50
Correlation metric: Peak-to-Correlation Energy (PCE)
Authentication threshold: PCE > 60
Tampering localization block: 128×128 pixels
False alarm rate: 10⁻⁵
Minimum image size: 256×256 pixels
accuracy: 99.7% camera identification accuracy at PCE > 60 (Lukáš et al., 2006). AI-generated image detection: 97–99% (no PRNU signal). Tampering localization: F1-score of 0.90 at 128×128 block resolution. False positive rate: < 0.001% at PCE threshold of 60. Performance degrades with fewer than 30 reference images.
source: Lukáš, J., Fridrich, J. & Goljan, M. (2006). Digital Camera Identification from Sensor Pattern Noise. IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 1(2), 205–214.
useCase: Identifying the specific camera device that captured a photograph. Detecting AI-generated images by absence of sensor fingerprint. Localizing tampered regions within authentic photographs. Linking multiple photographs to the same camera for forensic investigations.
strengths:
• PRNU fingerprint is unique per sensor — the gold standard for camera identification
• AI-generated images categorically fail PRNU authentication
• PCE test provides rigorous statistical framework with controlled false alarm rate
• Works after moderate JPEG compression, resizing, and social media processing
• Block-wise analysis enables tampering localization
limitations:
• Requires multiple reference images from the same camera for reliable estimation
• Image stabilization, HDR, and computational photography disrupt PRNU patterns
• Counter-forensic attacks can remove or forge PRNU (though detectable with advanced methods)
• Flat-field, saturated, or very dark images provide weak PRNU signal
• Geometric transformations (crop, rotate) require synchronization before correlation
